| 09:50–10:25 | Vedran Dunjko<br>Institution: Leiden University, The Netherlands<br>Title: The Provable Frontier of Quantum Machine Learning<br>Abstract: Quantum machine learning is shifting from proposing quantum models to determining precisely when quantum resources can improve learning. I will survey recent progress at this frontier: rigorous separations between quantum and classical learners, advantages enabled by quantum data or privileged quantum information, and generative models combining classical trainability with quantumly intractable sampling. Particular attention will be paid to the assumptions, access models and classical benchmarks underlying these results. Finally, I will ponder how these theoretical advances might be translated into useful methods for the biological and life sciences. |
| 10:25–10:55 | *Coffee break* |
| 10:55–11:30 | Miguel A. González Ballester<br>Institution: Universitat Pompeu Fabra (UPF), Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC) and ICREA, Barcelona, Spain<br>Title: Quantum computing for interpretable AI in healthcare<br>Abstract: Deep learning has had a profound effect in all walks of life, not least in medical research. The impressive performance of these methods is partly due to the development of very efficient approaches to solve highly overparameterized neural networks. Conversely, this leads to the problem of trust and interpretability of these complex models, which are key aspects in the medical domain. In this talk, we will see several works performed in our lab focusing on explainability and uncertainty modelling for a variety of clinical applications. We will then delve into the interface between machine learning and quantum computing, and explore early works on the development of quantum machine learning approaches for healthcare. First, we will show some results on the establishment of quantum diffusion models for medical image analysis. Finally, we will link back to explainability, formulating a quantum annealing framework for explainable deep learning. |
| 11:30–12:05 | Federico Ricci-Tersenghi<br>Institution: Sapienza University of Rome, Department of Physics, Italy<br>Title: Spin glass models are good benchmarks for discrete combinatorial optimization<br>Abstract: I will present a short survey of spin glass models which have been used as benchmarks for discrete combinatorial optimization problems.<br><br>I will summarize what is theoretically known about these spin glass models, stressing how the nature of the phase transition affects the hardness of the optimization problem.<br><br>I will show the performance of some classes of classical algorithms looking for ground states, with a special focus on the scaling with the problem size. |
| 12:05–12:30 | Daniel J. Egger<br>Institution: IBM Research Europe, Zurich, Switzerland<br>Title: The Quantum Optimization Benchmarking Library<br>Abstract: Recent progress has brought benchmarking of (heuristic) quantum algorithms at scale within reach. Particularly in combinatorial optimization, it is key to empirically analyze and track progress towards quantum advantage. This work introduces a systematic, fair and comparable benchmarking framework for quantum optimization methods by presenting ten model-independent problem classes that are challenging for classical methods. Track records of specific instances and solutions are given in an accompanying open-source repository. While the individual properties of the problem classes vary, they all become challenging from less than 100 to, at most, an order of 100,000 decision variables. We reference results from state-of-the-art solvers for instances across all problem classes and demonstrate exemplary baseline results obtained with quantum solvers for selected problems, which illustrate standardized benchmark reporting. The presented problem instances may be approached with classical or quantum algorithms executed on varying hardware platforms to drive the field towards quantum advantage. |

| 14:20–14:40 | Guglielmo Mazzola<br>Institution: SISSA, Trieste, Italy<br>Title: From Asymptotic Speedups to Practical Quantum Advantage<br>Abstract: Textbook quantum algorithms such as Grover's search—and, more generally, conventional quantum walks—offer compelling asymptotic speedups. Yet these speedups may fail to translate into practical quantum advantage when performance is measured in absolute runtime and compared with the best classical methods. Beyond assumptions concerning data access and input/output costs, the relatively low clock rates of fault-tolerant logical gates can push the crossover to quantum advantage far beyond practically relevant timescales [1].<br><br>In this talk, I will briefly review these conceptual and practical challenges. I will then introduce a new family of fully quantum Metropolis walks for sampling from classical dense-graph models [2]. By using a quantum-native proposal mechanism rather than quantizing a classically efficient Markov chain, these walks achieve speedups beyond the conventional quadratic limit. End-to-end resource estimates indicate a six-order-of-magnitude reduction in the crossover runtime—from roughly one thousand years for conventional quantum walks to less than one day—providing a promising route toward practical fault-tolerant quantum advantage.<br><br>References<br>[1] A. Maurizio and G. Mazzola, "Quantum Computing for Genomics: Conceptual Challenges and Practical Perspectives," PRX Life 3, 047001 (2025).<br>[2] M. Incudini and G. Mazzola, "Practical Advantage Beyond the Quadratic Speedup Limit with Fully-Quantum Walks," arXiv:2607.22818 [quant-ph] (2026). |
| 14:40–15:00 | Zev Kronenberg<br>Institution: PacBio, USA<br>Title: Developing a genomic standard using the Platinum Pedigree<br>Abstract: We combined multiple DNA-sequencing technologies with inheritance patterns from a large family to build a highly accurate map of human genetic variation. This benchmark covers most of the genome, including previously difficult regions, and provides a reference for measuring and improving computational methods that detect genetic differences. |
| 15:00–15:20 | Aurora Maurizio<br>Institution: Centre for Omics Sciences, IRCCS Ospedale San Raffaele, Milan, Italy<br>Title: Where genomics resists quantum speedup: a biologist's POV<br>Abstract: Quantum computing is increasingly promoted as a future accelerant for omics science, yet practical biological data constraints frequently complicate this narrative. Taking a biology-first perspective on our recent review (Maurizio & Mazzola, PRX Life, 2025), this talk examines the everyday realities of computational genomics to establish common ground before asking what a quantum-amenable biological problem would look like. I discuss how the size and error profile of sequencing data undercut naive database-search speedups; why problems that are hard in theory are often tractable in practice by classical heuristics; the limitations of classical machine learning; and the gap between omics data abundance and the scarcity of accessible real-world clinical benchmark datasets for testing the utility of quantum machine learning.<br><br>The goal is to identify the narrow niches where quantum methods can offer a genuine edge over strong classical baselines, and to argue that meaningful progress requires closer collaboration between domain experts in both quantum and biological sciences. |
| 15:20–15:40 | Miguel Ponce de Leon<br>Institution: Barcelona Supercomputing Centre, Spain<br>Title: Hard Optimization Problems in Mechanistic Biology<br>Abstract: Mechanistic models provide a powerful framework for translating biological knowledge into computational models that can be used to understand and predict the dynamics of complex biological systems. However, the construction and use of these models often lead to challenging optimization problems with very different computational characteristics. In this talk, I will discuss examples from systems and computational biology spanning three stages of mechanistic modelling. First, network inference, where incomplete biological knowledge can be formulated as constrained discrete optimization problems. Examples include reconstructing genome-scale metabolic networks and extracting context-specific models compatible with a given expression profile, which can be formulated as MILP-based set-covering problems. These intracellular networks capture the molecular machinery of individual cells, but modelling tissues and tumours additionally requires population heterogeneity, spatial organization and temporal dynamics. This motivates multiscale, hybrid models in which reconstructed mechanisms are embedded within larger-scale simulations. Second, parameter inference and model calibration, where parameter configurations must be identified from experimental observations, often using parallel simulation-based evolutionary algorithms. Third, intervention optimization, where such models can be used to search for effective treatment strategies, such as drug doses, combinations and schedules, through repeated simulation and parallel heuristic optimization. These problems range from combinatorial optimization with multiple feasible or optimal solutions to expensive, nonlinear and potentially stochastic simulation-based optimization. I will discuss how their biological structure and computational properties can inform the design of reproducible benchmark instances, with suitable objectives, constraints and classical baselines. Finally, I will consider how such problems could provide challenging and biologically meaningful test cases for emerging optimization approaches, including quantum and hybrid quantum-classical methods. |
| 15:40–16:10 | *Coffee break* |
| 16:10–16:30 | Francesco Zamponi<br>Institution: Sapienza University of Rome, Department of Physics, Italy<br>Title: Machine-Learning-Enhanced Monte Carlo for Combinatorial Optimization and Sampling<br>Abstract: Combinatorial optimization problems are central to both practical applications and the development of optimization methods.<br><br>While classical and quantum algorithms have been refined over decades, machine learning--assisted approaches are comparatively recent and have not yet consistently outperformed simple, state-of-the-art classical methods. I will discuss a class of Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) problems, specifically the challenge of finding minimum energy configurations in three-dimensional Ising spin glasses. I will discuss a Global Annealing Monte Carlo algorithm that integrates standard local moves with global moves proposed via machine learning. Benchmarking against Simulated Annealing and Population Annealing, I will show that Global Annealing not only surpasses the performance of Simulated Annealing but also exhibits greater robustness than Population Annealing, maintaining effectiveness across problem hardness and system size without hyperparameter tuning. These results provide clear and robust evidence that a machine learning--assisted optimization method can exceed the capabilities of classical state-of-the-art techniques in a combinatorial optimization setting. I will also discuss some applications of the algorithm to sampling configurations at low temperatures. |
| 16:30–16:50 | Gabriele Spada<br>Institution: CINECA, Italy<br>Title: Quantum Molecular Docking with Neutral Atoms at CINECA<br>Abstract: CINECA occupies a strategic position in Europe's quantum computing landscape, serving both as infrastructure provider and application developer. Through EuroQHPC-I, CINECA is hosting Sol: a neutral-atom system integrated with the Leonardo supercomputer. In QEC4QEA, CINECA leads the molecular docking use case.<br><br>We present our approach to quantum molecular docking, a computational method central to pharmaceutical drug discovery. We map molecular docking configurations to graph optimization problems that align naturally with neutral-atom hardware capabilities. The work leverages the inherent connection between Maximum Independent Set problems and Rydberg state physics, enabling efficient problem encoding on this emerging hardware architecture. |
| 16:50–17:10 | Diego Reforgiato Recupero<br>Institution: University of Cagliari, Department of Mathematics and Computer Science, Italy<br>Title: From Healthcare to Smart Grids: Exploring Optimization Problems and Quantum Solutions<br>Abstract: Optimization problems arise across many real-world domains, where complex constraints and large search spaces make the identification of effective solutions increasingly challenging. This talk explores these challenges through two application scenarios: healthcare and smart grids.<br><br>The first part introduces the Home Health Care Routing and Scheduling Problem (HHCRSP), a complex combinatorial optimization problem involving the assignment and scheduling of caregivers while accounting for skills, patient time windows, and synchronization and precedence constraints.<br><br>The second part focuses on smart grids and the problem of scheduling flexible energy loads to minimize prosumers' daily energy costs. As the number of flexible loads increases, the search space grows exponentially. A quantum formulation based on Grover's algorithm is presented to explore this search space and identify improved load-shifting configurations.<br><br>Through these two use cases, the talk highlights the complexity of real-world optimization and explores the potential of quantum computing as an emerging paradigm for addressing challenging combinatorial problems. |
| 17:10–17:30 | Carlo Mancini Terracciano<br>Institution: Sapienza University of Rome, Department of Physics, Italy<br>Title: From Neural Network Dose Estimation to Clinically Constrained Plans: Radiotherapy Treatment Planning as a Benchmark for Hybrid Optimization<br>Abstract: Radiotherapy treatment planning is a high-impact optimization problem in which beam geometry, particle energies, and fluences must be selected to deliver a prescribed dose to a target volume while sparing multiple organs at risk. Beyond its clinical relevance, the problem provides a challenging optimization benchmark: it combines a large continuous search space, strong non-convexities, expensive high-fidelity physical evaluations, and clinical objectives and constraints that may introduce non-smooth features in the optimization landscape.<br><br>We present an end-to-end optimization pipeline for proton therapy based on a frozen Graph U-Net surrogate that predicts three-dimensional dose deposition for individual pencil beams. A differentiable geometrical mapping transfers and accumulates these predictions on the patient computed tomography (CT), preserving gradients with respect to treatment parameters. This enables the joint optimization of beam geometry, pencil-beam energies and fluences, and spatial beam parameters. Our current classical hybrid baseline combines the global, derivative-free exploration of CMA-ES with gradient-based local refinement, exploiting the differentiability of both the neural surrogate and the geometrical mapping.<br><br>The framework has been tested from controlled phantom configurations to heterogeneous CT geometries, where the optimizer produces plans satisfying target-coverage and organ-at-risk constraints. We also present recent extensions to clinical CT data, highlighting the additional optimization challenges arising in realistic anatomies.<br><br>Beyond the specific application, proton therapy planning provides a test bed for studying the interaction between surrogate accuracy, global exploration, differentiable local optimization, and clinical constraints. It therefore offers a concrete benchmark for comparing optimization strategies in terms of solution quality, constraint satisfaction, robustness, computational budget, and sensitivity to surrogate-model errors. |
| 17:30–17:50 | Sergio Consoli<br>Institution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (JRC), Unit F.7, Ispra (VA), Italy<br>Title: On the Minimum Quartet Tree Cost problem for the quartet method of hierarchical clustering<br>Abstract: Given a set of n data objects and their pairwise distances, the Minimum Quartet Tree Cost (MQTC) problem seeks an optimal full unrooted binary tree by minimizing the sum of costs across all consistent embedded quartet topologies. The MQTC problem provides a powerful framework for hierarchical clustering without requiring strong prior structural assumptions, making it particularly valuable in health technologies and computational biology for constructing phylogenetic trees, analyzing viral/bacterial genomes, and classifying unknown pathogens into distinct groups or classes.<br><br>Because MQTC is an NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem, scalable exact solution approaches remain a challenge. This talk will present a summary of existing metaheuristics for MQTC alongside a foundational exact solution algorithm that generates exact gold-standard benchmarks for small problem sizes. Importantly, the underlying structural construction mechanisms of these MQTC solution algorithms present compelling properties for quantum algorithmic design. The presenter highlights MQTC as an ideal candidate benchmark problem for testing exact small-scale quantum optimization approaches and quantum routing. Finally, it is suggested to explore potential pathways toward efficient quantum methods—either through quantum-native formulations of existing MQTC metaheuristics or hybrid classical-quantum exact algorithms. |
